wa_mount_fury_east_direct_east_ridge._requested_as: wa_mount_fury_east_ridge (no such id in the DB; this is the Direct East Ridge on Mount Fury East Peak)

bivy.name: Access Creek Basin
bivy.water: Access Creek runs through the basin, plus meltwater off the snow above it; dependable all season
bivy.capacity: Open talus and brush with room for a small party — parties describe picking a flat patch rather than using established sites
bivy.permit: Overnight camping anywhere inside North Cascades National Park needs a National Park Service backcountry permit, and cross-country camps must be on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows, and at least 100 ft back from water
bivy.notes: Where the Access Creek bushwhack finally lets go of you and opens onto talus, roughly 1,900 ft above the Big Beaver crossing. Parties reaching it late on day one commonly reported arriving around 7pm. It is the last water before the long, shadeless scree chute to Access Col, and the usual place to stash bushwhacking gear and spare fuel before going high. Not a pretty camp — deadfall, brush and biting insects — but flat, watered and low, which is what matters after devil's club and huckleberry. Coming out, it is also the target that keeps the descent from turning into an epic.

bivy.name: Luna Col (Luna Pass)
bivy.water: A snow patch sitting at the saddle is the only supply; it shrinks through the summer, so late-season parties should expect a shallow melt pool or nothing at all
bivy.capacity: A scatter of small bivy platforms among rock windbreaks — reports describe several cramped spots and only one genuinely comfortable one
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required; the col sits in the Luna cross-country zone, which the park caps at six people per party and six parties per night
bivy.notes: The high camp for summit day, reached after the notorious steep heather-and-talus traverse from Access Col. The ground is glacier-polished slab with very little truly flat tent space, so most parties bivy rather than pitch. Being a saddle, it takes wind from either side with nothing to hide behind — one party woke at midnight to their cook pot being blown around, and got rain and blown grit before dawn. From here the Direct East Ridge still means dropping east, a long traverse around the 6,300-6,600 ft level and an ascending traverse to the 7,050 ft notch, so this is the only shelter you will see until you are back.

wa_luna_peak_southeast_slopes._requested_as: wa_luna_peak_standard (no such id; Southeast Slopes is Luna Peak's standard route)

bivy.name: Luna Camp (Big Beaver Trail)
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek, right there and reliable
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp with a fixed number of sites; your permit itinerary names the camp and the night
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for every overnight in the park complex, picked up from the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount; Luna Camp is a designated site, not cross-country ground
bivy.notes: The signed camp about 8 miles up the Big Beaver Trail from the boat landing, in old-growth cedar and only modestly above lake level. It is a trail camp, not a mountain one, and it earns its place because the water-taxi timetable often puts you on the trail late. From here it is another 1.5 miles north to the easy-to-miss boot path that leaves the trail just above the Access Creek confluence, so sleeping here sets you up to start the bushwhack fresh rather than at dusk.

bivy.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
bivy.water: Access Creek at the head of the drainage; reliable, but it is the last water until lingering snowmelt higher up
bivy.capacity: Open basin ground; parties describe it as pleasant camping for a small group rather than a set of established sites
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. Cross-country camping is only allowed on durable surfaces — snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadows, and never within 100 ft of water
bivy.notes: The open basin at the top of the Access Creek approach, roughly 1,700 ft above Luna Camp and the standard base for the peak. Getting here is the hard part: valley-bottom devil's club, a crossing to the north bank, then a swap back to the south side near 3,700-3,800 ft where cairns and a faint path use talus benches to duck the worst slide alder. Reports put the bushwhack alone at around three hours on the way out. From camp the climb goes up talus gullies southwest to a gap in the ridge, south of Point 6,730 on heather benches, then across the basin at about 6,600 ft to Luna Col at 7,200 ft — some 4,000 ft of gain, all of it above the last dependable water, so tank up before leaving.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.water: Streams run through the basin off the snowfields above and are dependable in a normal season, though heavy with glacial silt — filter and treat. In a heavy snow year the flow can be buried and parties have had to hunt a few hundred feet below camp for water coming off an outcrop
bivy.capacity: Several tent spots on gravel and rock in the basin flats, plus a bivy platform sized for two; the Terror Basin cross-country zone is capped at six parties a night and six people per party
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for the Terror Basin cross-country zone. Terror Basin is not one of the six zones that take advance reservations, so the permit is walk-up. Pitch on gravel, rock or snow — camping in meadows or within 100 ft of water is not allowed
bivy.notes: The base camp for the whole Southern Pickets and the one this route is built around: parties sleep here, climb, and come back to it, so plan two nights rather than moving camp. It sits about 400 ft below the 6,200 ft saddle the approach crosses, with flowers, running water and a full view of the range. The approach to it is roughly 7 miles and 6,000 ft of gain with no water at all on the last 3,500 ft, so fill up at the 1,600 ft crossing on Goodell Creek. From camp, the East Ridge is reached across heather and slabs and then the Terror Glacier below Inspiration's south side, which is low-angle but genuinely crevassed — rope up and carry rescue gear even though it is a short crossing.

wa_mount_terror_west_ridge._requested_as: wa_mount_terror_south_face (no such id; published sources describe the West Ridge / South Gully as Terror's standard line, approached from Crescent Creek Basin)

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.water: Silty streams running through the basin from the snowfields above; reliable in a normal season, filter and treat
bivy.capacity: Several sites on gravel and rock plus a two-person bivy platform; the zone allows six parties a night, six people per party
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Terror Basin cross-country zone; walk-up only, not reservable
bivy.notes: The usual first night for parties heading to Terror, about 400 ft below the 6,200 ft saddle at the top of the Goodell Creek boot path. It is not the camp you climb Terror from — from here you still have to traverse and cross the roughly 6,400 ft saddle by the Chopping Block and drop into Crescent Creek Basin — but it is the natural place to stop after 6,000 ft of gain, and parties who lose the light on the approach routinely take it as-is.

bivy.name: Chopping Block saddle camp
bivy.water: None at the saddle itself. The nearest reported source on the way in is a small stream around 5,700 ft on the granite slabs below, so carry water up
bivy.capacity: Small; reports describe a single good spot on the saddle rather than a cluster of sites
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required; the Crescent Creek cross-country zone is capped at six parties a night and six people per party
bivy.notes: The saddle on the Chopping Block ridge overlooking Crescent Creek Basin, and the camp parties rate most highly on this side of the range — an open grandstand on the Southern Pickets. It is a dry, exposed perch, so the trade is view and position against carrying your water. Being on the crest it also puts you above the basin, which means a downclimb of a couple of hundred feet to get onto the climbing terrain each morning.

bivy.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
bivy.water: Streams coming off the slabs above the basin — one party found two of them beside their site; snowmelt-fed, so check rather than assume late in a dry season
bivy.capacity: Small flat pockets rather than one site; parties report hunting among rock and heather outcrops before settling, and one describes checking six or eight before finding a bench that was only marginally good enough
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required for the Crescent Creek cross-country zone, capped at six parties a night and six people per party. Camp on rock, snow or bare ground only, and keep 100 ft from the streams
bivy.notes: The working camp for Terror, in the basin under the peak. Published camps sit between roughly 6,000 and 6,200 ft — there is talk among parties of a named 'Crescent Camp' that several have gone looking for and not found, so treat this as a zone of flat spots rather than a fixed site. Getting here from Terror Basin means crossing the upper Barrier or the roughly 6,400 ft saddle by the Chopping Block and downclimbing a couple of hundred feet of loose class 3 into the basin, which is a real piece of ground in fog. Rodents have been reported working the rocks at dusk, so hang or armour your food. Times from this camp are long: parties report about seven hours up and four and a half back on Terror.

bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet streams; the trail up also crosses reliable side creeks
bivy.capacity: Established sites in the cirque below the east face, enough for several parties
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness has no backcountry permit or quota — sign the trailhead register and carry a recreation pass where the trailhead requires one. There is a Forest Service closure to overnight camping and to campfires within 200 ft of the Holden Lake shoreline, so pitch back from the water
bivy.notes: The obvious camp about 4 miles up the Holden Lake Trail from its junction with the Railroad Creek Trail, sitting in a cirque right under Bonanza's east face. Easy to reach, water everywhere, and the last comfortable ground before the tread fades. The catch is insects: parties consistently describe black flies between roughly 3,000 and 4,000 ft on the way up and serious mosquitoes from the lake upward, with one report calling it the worst they had met anywhere in Washington. Camping here also leaves an extra 1,000 ft to climb on summit day compared with going on to the pass.

bivy.name: Holden Pass
bivy.water: Snow patches at and near the pass, which is often melting rather than running; the pass itself is largely dry, so several parties filled at the last switchback below and others simply melted snow at camp
bivy.capacity: Room for a small group — one party of six used a flat area near the pass, and another found a dry site a short way west of the crest
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit or quota in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register, and note the 200 ft camping and campfire closure at Holden Lake below
bivy.notes: The standard high camp, reached from the lake by a rough hillside traverse northwest — the tread above the outlet fades into slide alder and talus and is genuinely brushy early season with high water. Reported times from Holden Village run from under 4 hours to about 5. It buys you 1,000 ft off summit day and noticeably fewer mosquitoes than the lake, though parties still describe them as bad. It is a pass, so expect wind and weather with nothing to hide behind; one party sat out a midnight lightning storm here. Above camp the route makes a rising traverse west to a snowfield around 7,000-7,300 ft and class 3 waterfall slabs — go high and right of the water — before the Mary Green Glacier.

bivy.name: Bivy below the waterfall slabs
bivy.water: Running water close by, from the same waterfall drainage the slabs are named for
bivy.capacity: A single ledge, sized for a small party
bivy.permit: No permit needed; standard Glacier Peak Wilderness rules apply
bivy.notes: A ledge camp reported around 6,900 ft, above Holden Pass and just below the waterfall slabs that lead onto the glacier. The party that used it went higher specifically to escape the mosquitoes at the pass and rated it well for bugs, views and water. It is a bivy rather than a campsite, and it commits you to descending the slabs late in the day when they are wetter and less friendly than in the morning. Only one published account of it, so treat the ground as unconfirmed and have the pass as a fallback.

bivy.name: Holden Village ballfield campground
bivy.capacity: A developed campground beside the village
bivy.permit: Village property rather than wilderness; the ferry and bus schedule to Lucerne and Holden governs when you can arrive and leave, and the village runs on cash
bivy.notes: The campground on the edge of Holden Village, about a mile back down the road from where the climb starts. Not part of the climb, but it is what parties use on either side of the ferry timetable — several reports mention sleeping here after coming off the mountain and waiting for the boat, in mosquitoes that are present but tolerable.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest camp
bivy.capacity: Small forest sites; the Forest Service notes camping spots around mile 3 on the Downey Creek Trail and again at the Bachelor Creek end near mile 6.6
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no backcountry permit or quota; sign the trailhead register. A recreation pass such as the Northwest Forest Pass is honoured for the fee at the Downey Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: A timbered camp on the creek partway up the Bachelor Creek leg, used by parties who lose the day to the brush, blowdown and washed-out sections below. It is a bail-out night rather than a plan: car to Cub Lake is commonly reported at 9-11 hours, and the section above Bachelor Creek climbs steeply and crosses avalanche paths under Spire Point that need assessing in early-season snow.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.water: The lake and the basin's streams; plentiful
bivy.capacity: A well-established camp with room for several parties, though the meadows around Cub and Itswoot Lakes have been heavily worn and camping there is discouraged in favour of the ridge above
bivy.permit: No permit or quota in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register and carry a recreation pass for the trailhead. Standard Leave No Trace practice here means using existing hardened sites rather than making new ones in the meadow
bivy.notes: The lake camp at the top of the Bachelor Creek climb, reached after a drop of several hundred feet into the basin that most parties find unwelcome at the end of a long day. Water and flat ground are easy, which is why it gets used, but the meadows show it and the better-positioned option is the ridge another 900 ft above. If you sleep here, summit day starts with that climb.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.water: A substantial creek near the ridge sites, fed by snow well above, plus running water at the ridge camp itself; snowmelt-dependent, so verify late season
bivy.capacity: Good open camping along the crest for several parties
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit needed in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register
bivy.notes: The camp parties call the best on this approach, on the ridge crest roughly 900 ft above Cub Lake, with the lakes below and the Ptarmigan country opening out. Water is at hand and the ground is good. Expect mosquitoes. Moving up here from the lake costs about an hour but is the sensible split, since the guidebook figure from the ridge to the summit is 6-9 hours and parties report 6-8. From camp the route crosses the south ridge toward Spire Point, drops about 200 ft, and traverses cairned but unmarked ground below cliff bands over polished slabs to the foot of the Dome Glacier.

bivy.name: Dome-Dana col
bivy.capacity: Small; one report records two parties camped there at once
bivy.permit: No permit or quota in Glacier Peak Wilderness
bivy.notes: A high perch around 7,300 ft used by parties who want to shorten summit day or who are linking the Ptarmigan Traverse. It puts you above the traverse and its route-finding, with the upper Dome Glacier — which parties describe as mellow — immediately above. The trade is no running water and full exposure; the ridge camp lower down is the more common choice, and pushing this high is generally judged not to save enough time to be worth it.
